title: Composition-Grounded Data Synthesis for Visual Reasoning
claim: Decompose a few seed examples into reusable primitive factors, then recombine them with new inputs to synthesize many diverse compositional examples.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, factor word cloud merging with new images into outputs
description: Three-stage left-to-right diagram. The left blue-bordered panel, titled 'Seed Dataset', shows sample seed questions (e.g. 'Which ... is greater?') with small chart thumbnails: bar, pie and line charts. Each is paired with a reasoning graph of colored nodes: red for perception, pink for calculation, blue for fact checking. A legend sits at the bottom right. The middle panel, 'Factors', shows a word cloud of terms such as perception, calculation, comparison and fact checking, scattered with colored dots. A plus sign joins it to 'Another Image Source', a grid of new chart images. An orange bracket and arrow lead to the right orange-bordered panel, 'COGS Synthetic Dataset'. That panel has four rows, each with a chart, a new question header, a recombined node graph, and gray subquestion text.
caption: COGS: Starting from a small set of reasoning-intensive seed questions, COGS decomposes them into primitive perception and reasoning factors, which are then recombined with new image sources to synthesize question–answer pairs. This process expands both the quantity and diversity of reasoning types beyond the original seeds. Fig. 2 shows an illustrative example.
abstract: Pretrained multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) demonstrate strong performance on diverse multimodal tasks, but remain limited in reasoning capabilities for domains where annotations are difficult to collect. In this work, we focus on artificial image domains such as charts, rendered documents, and webpages, which are abundant in practice yet lack large-scale human annotated reasoning datasets. We introduce COGS (COmposition-Grounded data Synthesis), a data-efficient framework for equipping MLLMs with advanced reasoning abilities from a small set of seed questions. The key idea is to decompose each seed question into primitive perception and reasoning factors, which can then be systematically recomposed with new images to generate large collections of synthetic question-answer pairs. Each generated question is paired with subquestions and intermediate answers, enabling reinforcement learning with factor-level process rewards. Experiments on chart reasoning show that COGS substantially improves performance on unseen questions, with the largest gains on reasoning-heavy and compositional questions. Moreover, training with a factor-level mixture of different seed data yields better transfer across multiple datasets, suggesting that COGS induces generalizable capabilities rather than dataset-specific overfitting. We further demonstrate that the framework extends beyond charts to other domains such as webpages.
